claim: PyronicSF is a GFP-based sensor with improved dynamic range for pyruvate detection
source: Here we introduce PyronicSF, a user-friendly GFP-based sensor of improved dynamic range that enables real-time subcellular quantitation of mitochondrial pyruvate transport, concentration and flux.
evidence: The abstract directly states the development and characteristics of PyronicSF

claim: Cultured mouse astrocytes maintain mitochondrial pyruvate in the low micromolar range
source: We report that cultured mouse astrocytes maintain mitochondrial pyruvate in the low micromolar range, below cytosolic pyruvate, which means that the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier MPC is poised to exert ultrasensitive control on the balance between respiration and anaplerosis/gluconeogenesis.
evidence: Direct measurement using PyronicSF sensor in cultured astrocytes

claim: Mitochondrial pyruvate is below cytosolic pyruvate in cultured mouse astrocytes
source: We report that cultured mouse astrocytes maintain mitochondrial pyruvate in the low micromolar range, below cytosolic pyruvate, which means that the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier MPC is poised to exert ultrasensitive control on the balance between respiration and anaplerosis/gluconeogenesis.
evidence: Comparative measurements of pyruvate in different cellular compartments

claim: The MPC is poised to exert ultrasensitive control on the balance between respiration and anaplerosis/gluconeogenesis
source: We report that cultured mouse astrocytes maintain mitochondrial pyruvate in the low micromolar range, below cytosolic pyruvate, which means that the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier MPC is poised to exert ultrasensitive control on the balance between respiration and anaplerosis/gluconeogenesis.
evidence: Inference based on measured pyruvate concentrations and mathematical modeling

claim: PyronicSF is functional in living tissue of Drosophila melanogaster larvae brain
source: The functionality of the sensor in living tissue is demonstrated in the brain of Drosophila melanogaster larvae.
evidence: Experimental demonstration in fly larvae brain tissue

claim: Mitochondria account for over 90% of ATP production in animal cells
source: Mitochondria are the chief energy generators of animal cells, accounting for over 90% of ATP production, and they also generate building blocks for the synthesis of sugars, amino acids, nucleic acids and prosthetic groups, essential elements for tissue growth, plasticity and regeneration.

claim: Mitochondria generate building blocks for the synthesis of sugars, amino acids, nucleic acids and prosthetic groups
source: Mitochondria are the chief energy generators of animal cells, accounting for over 90% of ATP production, and they also generate building blocks for the synthesis of sugars, amino acids, nucleic acids and prosthetic groups, essential elements for tissue growth, plasticity and regeneration.

claim: Pyruvate is a major mitochondrial substrate for mammalian cells
source: A major mitochondrial substrate for mammalian cells is pyruvate, a 3-carbon organic acid produced from glucose, lactate and amino acids.

claim: Pyruvate is a 3-carbon organic acid produced from glucose, lactate and amino acids
source: A major mitochondrial substrate for mammalian cells is pyruvate, a 3-carbon organic acid produced from glucose, lactate and amino acids.

claim: Extracellular pyruvate may reach the cytosol via monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs)
source: Extracellular pyruvate may also reach the cytosol via monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) (Halestrap and Price, 1999).

claim: Pyruvate enters mitochondria through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC)
source: Pyruvate enters mitochondria through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) (Halestrap and Denton, 1975; Herzig et al., 2012; Bricker et al., 2012).

claim: PyronicSF shows a strong increase in fluorescence when exposed to pyruvate in vitro
source: Exposure of the sensor to pyruvate in vitro caused a strong increase in fluorescence when excited by blue light (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct experimental observation with purified protein

claim: PyronicSF excited at 488 nm shows approximately 250% increase in fluorescence emission with a KD of 480 μM
source: Excited at 488 nm, the increase in fluorescence emission was ≈ 250%, with a KD of 480 μM (Figure 1C).

claim: PyronicSF is insensitive to lactate and other structurally related organic acids
source: As expected from the behavior of PdhR (San Martín et al., 2014a) in the FRET sensor Pyronic, PyronicSF was insensitive to lactate, to other structurally related organic acids, and to NAD+ and NADH (Figure 1D).

claim: PyronicSF is insensitive to NAD+ and NADH
source: As expected from the behavior of PdhR (San Martín et al., 2014a) in the FRET sensor Pyronic, PyronicSF was insensitive to lactate, to other structurally related organic acids, and to NAD+ and NADH (Figure 1D).

claim: The sensing of pyruvate by PyronicSF is not affected by pH, but there is a pH-dependent shift of the dose-response curve
source: While the sensing of pyruvate by PyronicSF was not affected by pH, there was a pH-dependent shift of the dose-response curve (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental characterization at different pH values

claim: The fluorescence ratio of the sensor Pyronic is insensitive to pH in the physiological range
source: Because the fluorescence ratio of the sensor Pyronic is insensitive to pH in the physiological range (San Martín et al., 2014a), we attribute the effect of pH on PyronicSF to the pH-sensitivity typical of cpGFPs (Marvin et al., 2013; Cambronne et al., 2016).

claim: The pH effect on PyronicSF is attributed to the pH-sensitivity typical of cpGFPs
source: Because the fluorescence ratio of the sensor Pyronic is insensitive to pH in the physiological range (San Martín et al., 2014a), we attribute the effect of pH on PyronicSF to the pH-sensitivity typical of cpGFPs (Marvin et al., 2013; Cambronne et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference based on known properties of cpGFPs cited from literature

claim: The amplitude of the response of PyronicSF was >6 times that of Pyronic in HEK293 cells
source: The amplitude of the response of PyronicSF was >6 times that of Pyronic (Figure 1E; San Martín et al., 2014a).

claim: PyronicSF was successfully targeted to the mitochondrial matrix using the destination sequence of cytochrome oxidase
source: PyronicSF was targeted to the mitochondrial matrix using the destination sequence of cytochrome oxidase. The targeting was successful in various cell types, as evidenced by the labeling of elongated cytoplasmic structures that are of shape and size characteristic of mitochondria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Mito-PyronicSF colocalized with the voltage-sensitive dye TMRM
source: Confirmation of correct targeting was provided by colocalization with the voltage-sensitive dye TMRM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Mito-PyronicSF colocalized with mCherry targeted to mitochondria
source: Mito-PyronicSF also colocalized with the red fluorescent protein mCherry targeted to mitochondria (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Exposure of astrocytes expressing mito-PyronicSF to pyruvate resulted in a reversible increase in fluorescence ratio
source: Exposure of astrocytes co-expressing mito-PyronicSF and mito-mCherry to pyruvate resulted in a reversible increase in fluorescence ratio, evidencing mitochondrial uptake (Figure 2B).

claim: The rise of pyruvate in mitochondria was much slower than its accumulation in the cytosol
source: The rise in mitochondria was much slower than its accumulation in the cytosol, monitored indirectly with PyronicSF targeted to the nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Comparative kinetic measurements in different compartments

claim: The uptake of pyruvate by mitochondria was sensitive to the specific MPC1 blocker UK-5099
source: The uptake of pyruvate by mitochondria was sensitive to the specific MPC1 blocker UK-5099 (Halestrap and Denton, 1975; Herzig et al., 2012; Bricker et al., 2012; Nagampalli et al., 2018; Figure 2C).

claim: The average degree of pyruvate uptake inhibition by UK-5099 was 69%
source: The average degree of uptake inhibition was 69% (Figure 2C).

claim: The insulin sensitizer rosiglitazone inhibited the uptake of pyruvate by astrocytic mitochondria by 67%
source: To illustrate the potential of mito-PyronicSF for drug discovery, we show here that the insulin sensitizer rosiglitazone inhibited the uptake of pyruvate by astrocytic mitochondria by 67% (Figure 2D), providing confirmation that MPC is a target of thiazolidinediones (Divakaruni et al., 2013).

claim: MPC is a target of thiazolidinediones
source: To illustrate the potential of mito-PyronicSF for drug discovery, we show here that the insulin sensitizer rosiglitazone inhibited the uptake of pyruvate by astrocytic mitochondria by 67% (Figure 2D), providing confirmation that MPC is a target of thiazolidinediones (Divakaruni et al., 2013).
evidence: Experimental confirmation of previously reported finding

claim: There is a 1:1 stoichiometry between proton and pyruvate transport by the MPC
source: Given the 1:1 stoichiometry between proton and pyruvate transport by the MPC, and the respective pH gradient between cytosol and mitochondria (7.2 and 7.8 [Azarias et al., 2011], equivalent to a 4-fold proton gradient), mitochondrial pyruvate may reside anywhere between a few micromolar and four times the cytosolic concentration of pyruvate, a quantity that is neither known with precision.
evidence: Cited from literature and theoretical consideration

claim: The pH gradient between cytosol and mitochondria is 7.2 and 7.8, equivalent to a 4-fold proton gradient
source: Given the 1:1 stoichiometry between proton and pyruvate transport by the MPC, and the respective pH gradient between cytosol and mitochondria (7.2 and 7.8 [Azarias et al., 2011], equivalent to a 4-fold proton gradient), mitochondrial pyruvate may reside anywhere between a few micromolar and four times the cytosolic concentration of pyruvate, a quantity that is neither known with precision.

claim: Steady-state mitochondrial pyruvate lies at the low end of the detection range of PyronicSF at extracellular levels of glucose, lactate and pyruvate found in brain tissue
source: At extracellular levels of glucose, lactate and pyruvate found in brain tissue, steady-state mitochondrial pyruvate was found to lie at the low end of the detection range of PyronicSF (Figure 3A and C), which is in agreement with parallel measurements using the FRET sensor (Figure 3B and C).

claim: Median mitochondrial pyruvate measured with PyronicSF was 21 μM
source: Using this protocol, median mitochondrial pyruvate measured with PyronicSF was 21 μM.

claim: Median steady-state concentration of pyruvate in the cytosol was 33 μM
source: Experiments with the sensor targeted to the cytosol showed that the median steady-state concentration of pyruvate in this compartment was 33 μM.

claim: Estimated with the FRET sensor, median pyruvate concentrations were 25 μM in mitochondria and 40 μM in cytosol
source: Estimated with the FRET sensor, whose KD is five times lower, median pyruvate concentrations were 25 μM in mitochondria and 40 μM in cytosol, a difference of 15 μM.

claim: Both PyronicSF and Pyronic sensors converged in showing that mitochondrial pyruvate is in the low micromolar range and lower than cytosolic pyruvate
source: Thus, both sensors converged in showing that mitochondrial pyruvate is in the low micromolar range, and that is lower than cytosolic pyruvate.
evidence: Convergent results from two different sensors

claim: Activation of PDH does not translate into a sustained flux increase because mitochondrial pyruvate becomes depleted
source: Firstly, activation of the MPC is necessary for efficient stimulation of oxidative metabolism. For example, PDH activation does not translate into a sustained flux increase because mitochondrial pyruvate becomes depleted, leading to partial PDH desaturation (Figure 3E).

claim: The fall of mitochondrial pyruvate leads to a strong decrease of flux through PC
source: More dramatically, the fall of pyruvate leads to a strong decrease of flux through PC, a 'steal' flux phenomenon.

claim: If steady-state concentration of mitochondrial pyruvate is below 30 μM, a given change in MPC activity will be amplified in terms of PC flux
source: Actually, Figure 3F shows that if the steady-state concentration of mitochondrial pyruvate is below 30 μM, a given change in MPC activity will be amplified in terms of PC flux, a phenomenon that has been termed ultrasensitivity (Ferrell and Ha, 2014).
evidence: Mathematical modeling analysis with citation to ultrasensitivity concept

claim: At 21 μM mitochondrial pyruvate, a 1% MPC increase causes a 1.2% increase in PC flux
source: For example, at 21 μM mitochondrial pyruvate, a 1% MPC increase causes a 1.2% increase in PC flux.

claim: At 21 μM mitochondrial pyruvate, a 1% MPC increase causes only a 0.4% increase in PDH flux
source: In contrast, PDH flux increases by only 0.4% (Figure 3F).

claim: The MPC and cytosolic pyruvate interact synergistically with respect to PC flux but antagonistically with respect to PDH flux
source: Remarkably, the MPC and cytosolic pyruvate interact synergistically with respect to PC flux but antagonistically with respect to PDH flux.

claim: A coincidental rise of MPC activity and cytosolic pyruvate will cause an increase in PC flux larger than the sum of the two independent effects
source: A coincidental rise of MPC activity and cytosolic pyruvate will cause an increase in PC flux larger than the sum of the two independent effects, but for PDH the effects are not even additive (Figure 3G).

claim: The MPC is poised for sensitive modulation of anaplerosis
source: Together, these results indicate that the MPC is poised for sensitive modulation of anaplerosis.
evidence: Inference from modeling results and experimental measurements

claim: MPC stoppage with UK-5099 caused immediate depletion of mitochondrial pyruvate
source: As shown in Figure 4A, MPC stoppage with UK-5099 caused immediate depletion of mitochondrial pyruvate.

claim: Long term exposure to UK-5099 causes irreversible inhibition of the MPC
source: Reportedly, long term exposure to UK-5099 causes irreversible inhibition of the MPC (Divakaruni et al., 2013; Hildyard et al., 2005) but this was not observed at the low concentrations and short exposure times used here (Figure 4B).
evidence: Cited from literature but contradicted by current experimental observations

claim: UK-5099 inhibition was reversible at the low concentrations and short exposure times used in this study
source: Reportedly, long term exposure to UK-5099 causes irreversible inhibition of the MPC (Divakaruni et al., 2013; Hildyard et al., 2005) but this was not observed at the low concentrations and short exposure times used here (Figure 4B).

claim: Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation strongly stimulated mitochondrial pyruvate consumption
source: Using such a protocol, uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) strongly stimulated mitochondrial pyruvate consumption (Figure 4C) whereas conversely, inhibition of OXPHOS with the cytochrome oxidase inhibitor azide resulted in a lower rate (Figure 4D).

claim: Inhibition of OXPHOS with the cytochrome oxidase inhibitor azide resulted in a lower rate of mitochondrial pyruvate consumption
source: Using such a protocol, uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) strongly stimulated mitochondrial pyruvate consumption (Figure 4C) whereas conversely, inhibition of OXPHOS with the cytochrome oxidase inhibitor azide resulted in a lower rate (Figure 4D).

claim: Mitochondrial pyruvate consumption rates ranged from 0.29 to 3.1 μM/s, with a median value of 1.1 μM/s
source: There was substantial variability between cells, which ranged from 0.29 to 3.1 μM/s, with a median value of 1.1 μM/s (Figure 4E).

claim: Steady-state pyruvate in peripheral mitochondria was higher than in mitochondria lying close to the nucleus
source: Steady-state pyruvate in a small group of peripheral mitochondria was found to be higher than in mitochondria lying close to the nucleus.
evidence: Subcellular spatial measurements within single cells

claim: Pyruvate consumption may differ within a cell between different mitochondrial populations
source: Application of the transporter-block protocol showed that pyruvate consumption may also differ within a cell (Figure 5).

claim: PyronicSF expressed very well in cytosol and mitochondria of perineurial glial cells in Drosophila melanogaster larvae
source: PyronicSF expressed very well in cytosol and mitochondria of these cells (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Imaging of sensor expression in fly tissue

claim: Superfusion of acutely isolated Drosophila brains with pyruvate resulted in a quick increase in cytosolic pyruvate
source: Superfusion of acutely isolated brains with pyruvate resulted in a quick increase in cytosolic pyruvate, revealing the presence of abundant surface pyruvate transporters in these cells (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Time-course measurements in fly brain tissue

claim: The response of mitochondria to pyruvate in Drosophila perineurial cells was slower and plateaued at lower pyruvate levels than cytosol
source: The response of mitochondria was slower and plateaued at lower pyruvate levels, consistent with mitochondria being a site of pyruvate consumption downstream of the cytosol (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: Comparative kinetic measurements in fly tissue

claim: In Drosophila perineurial glial cells, the steady-state level of pyruvate was much higher in the cytosol than in mitochondria
source: In the presence of a buffer containing glucose, lactate and pyruvate, the steady-state level of pyruvate was much higher in the cytosol than in mitochondria (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Comparative measurements in different compartments in fly tissue

claim: The steep transmitochondrial pyruvate gradient in Drosophila perineurial cells suggests that the MPC is a key regulator of the balance between catabolism and anabolism
source: Nevertheless, the steep transmitochondrial pyruvate gradient measured here suggests that the MPC is also a key regulator of the balance between catabolism and anabolism in perineurial glial cells.

claim: PyronicSF has a higher dynamic range than the original Pyronic sensor
source: The present sensor PyronicSF improves on the original sensor on several grounds: i. It has a higher dynamic range.
evidence: Comparative characterization of the two sensors

claim: PyronicSF does not require FRET detection technology
source: ii. It does not require FRET detection technology, so it can be used in standard wide-field and confocal microscopes.

claim: PyronicSF is smaller than Pyronic and therefore more easily targetable to subcellular domains
source: iii. It is smaller and therefore more easily targetable to subcellular domains.

claim: PyronicSF has lower affinity for pyruvate than Pyronic, providing an extended window for rate monitoring when expressed in mitochondria
source: iv. Because of its lower affinity for pyruvate, when expressed in mitochondria it provides an extended window for rate monitoring.
evidence: Comparison of sensor affinities and their implications

claim: PyronicSF permits monitoring pyruvate concentration, permeability and flux in individual mitochondria
source: vi. It permits monitoring pyruvate concentration, permeability and flux in individual mitochondria, thus offering a practical tool for the functional study of mitochondrial heterogeneity.

claim: PyronicSF is more sensitive than Pyronic at all pyruvate concentrations
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 5 shows that PyronicSF is more sensitive than Pyronic at all pyruvate concentrations.

claim: One limitation of PyronicSF is its pH sensitivity
source: One limitation of PyronicSF is its pH sensitivity, which can be corrected as explained in the Results Section.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation with proposed correction method

claim: Pyruvate in samples of brain tissue obtained by quick-freezing was measured at 99 μM
source: Pyruvate in samples of brain tissue obtained by quick-freezing was measured at 99 μM (Hawkins et al., 1973), although fast glycogen degradation during the procedure may have affected the result (Swanson et al., 1992; Oe et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous literature with caveat about methodology

claim: MPC inhibition mobilizes glutamate towards oxidation therefore ameliorating excitotoxicity in neurodegenerative diseases
source: The MPC has also been pinpointed as a target in neurodegenerative diseases, because its inhibition mobilizes glutamate towards oxidation therefore ameliorating excitotoxicity (Divakaruni et al., 2017).

claim: In cancer cells, MPC acts as a protective factor by inhibiting the Warburg effect
source: In contrast, in cancer cells, MPC acts as a protective factor by inhibiting the Warburg effect (Schell et al., 2014) and MPC inhibition enhanced tumor aggression and resistance to chemo- and radiotherapy (Schell et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017).

claim: MPC inhibition enhanced tumor aggression and resistance to chemo- and radiotherapy
source: In contrast, in cancer cells, MPC acts as a protective factor by inhibiting the Warburg effect (Schell et al., 2014) and MPC inhibition enhanced tumor aggression and resistance to chemo- and radiotherapy (Schell et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017).

claim: Growth under MPC-inhibition is sustained by reprogramming of mitochondrial metabolism including enhanced glutaminolysis and lipid catabolism
source: Growth under MPC-inhibition is sustained by reprogramming of mitochondrial metabolism including enhanced glutaminolysis and lipid catabolism (Vacanti et al., 2014).

claim: PyronicSF consists of the complete sequence of the bacterial transcription factor PdhR linked to a circularly-permuted version of GFP (cpGFP)
source: Figure 1A illustrates PyronicSF (Single Fluorophore), in which the complete sequence of the bacterial transcription factor PdhR (Quail and Guest, 1995) has been linked to a circularly-permuted version of GFP (cpGFP) (Nagai et al., 2001) (DNA sequence in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of sensor construction with citations

claim: PdhR is a transcriptional regulator from Escherichia coli that controls the expression of PDH
source: PdhR is a transcriptional regulator from Escherichia coli that controls the expression of PDH (Quail and Guest, 1995) and was previously used as a specific pyruvate-binding domain in the FRET sensor Pyronic (San Martín et al., 2014a).

claim: cpGFP is a variant of GFP in which the two ends of the protein are linked with the hexapeptide GGTGGS
source: The fluorophore cpGFP is a variant of GFP in which the two ends of the protein are linked with the hexapeptide GGTGGS, while new ends were generated by cleaving the protein between amino acid residues N144 and Y145 and replacing the latter by a methionine to serve as new N terminus (Baird et al., 1999).

claim: Three sensor variants were designed by inserting cpGFP after amino acid residues 94, 122 and 189 of PdhR
source: Using a 3D model structure of PdhR obtained with the M4T server 3.0 from Fiser Laboratory, three sensor variants were designed by inserting cpGFP after amino acid residues 94, 122 and 189 of PdhR, that is, within loops of the ligand binding domain with free access to solvent and far from the hydrophobic core of the protein.

claim: The variant with cpGFP inserted after amino acid residue 189 of PdhR showed the largest change in fluorescence intensity upon binding pyruvate
source: The variant with cpGFP inserted after the amino acid residue 189 of PdhR showed the largest change in fluorescence intensity upon binding pyruvate and was christened PyronicSF (PYRuvate Optical Nano-Indicator from CECs Single Fluorophore; DNA sequence is available in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Dead-PyronicSF is a version of the sensor with greatly reduced sensitivity to pyruvate and conserved sensitivity to pH
source: A version of the sensor with greatly reduced sensitivity to pyruvate and conserved sensitivity to pH (Dead-PyronicSF; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) was obtained by mutating the first linker CTCGAA (red in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, coding for Leu-Glu) to ACCATG (coding for Tre-Met).

claim: Four copies of the destination sequence were needed to target the FRET sensor Pyronic to mitochondria
source: The FRET sensor Pyronic could also be targeted to mitochondria in functional form (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but four copies of the destination sequence were needed, probably because of its larger size relative to PyronicSF.
evidence: Experimental observation with inference about mechanism

claim: The concentration of pyruvate in both mitochondria and cytosol varied between cells
source: The concentration of pyruvate in both compartments varied between cells, explained by differences between experiments (i.e. culture conditions), and also by heterogeneity within a given microscopic field (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: There was no apparent correlation between sensor expression level and mitochondrial pyruvate concentration
source: There was no apparent correlation between sensor expression level and mitochondrial pyruvate concentration (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: PyronicSF is capable of detecting a difference of 10 μM in the low micromolar range, provided that sufficient replicates are available
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 4 shows that the sensor is capable of detecting a difference of 10 μM in the low micromolar range, provided that sufficient replicates are available.
evidence: In vitro characterization of sensor sensitivity

claim: The combined flux of PDH and PC was set at 1.2 μM/s in the mathematical model
source: Their combined flux was set at 1.2 μM/s (Fernández-Moncada and Barros, 2014), with PDH and PC respectively accounting for 76% and 24% (Oz et al., 2004).
evidence: Model parameters based on cited literature

claim: PDH and PC respectively account for 76% and 24% of mitochondrial pyruvate flux
source: Their combined flux was set at 1.2 μM/s (Fernández-Moncada and Barros, 2014), with PDH and PC respectively accounting for 76% and 24% (Oz et al., 2004).
evidence: Model parameters based on cited literature

claim: The behavior of the system is essentially insensitive to the specific kinetic parameters of the MPC
source: Of note, the behavior of the system is essentially insensitive to the specific kinetic parameters of the MPC (data not shown), as expected for a transporter working far from thermodynamic equilibrium.

claim: There was no apparent correlation between sensor expression level and the rate of mitochondrial pyruvate consumption
source: There was no apparent correlation between sensor expression level and the rate of mitochondrial pyruvate consumption (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: Similar steady-states of pyruvate depletion were reached at 0.5 μM and 10 μM UK-5099
source: We do not think that the partial effect is explained by insufficient UK-5099, because similar steady-states were reached at 0.5 μM and 10 μM UK-5099 (53 ± 12% versus 47 ± 6%; 12 cells in three paired experiments, p>0.05, data not shown) and the half-inhibition constant for MPC inhibition by UK-5099 is only 50 nM (Halestrap, 1975).

claim: The half-inhibition constant for MPC inhibition by UK-5099 is only 50 nM
source: We do not think that the partial effect is explained by insufficient UK-5099, because similar steady-states were reached at 0.5 μM and 10 μM UK-5099 (53 ± 12% versus 47 ± 6%; 12 cells in three paired experiments, p>0.05, data not shown) and the half-inhibition constant for MPC inhibition by UK-5099 is only 50 nM (Halestrap, 1975).

claim: Pyronic has permitted high resolution measurement of pyruvate in multiple contexts from cultured cells to living animals
source: A few years ago, our group introduced the FRET sensor Pyronic (San Martín et al., 2014a) that has permitted high resolution measurement of pyruvate in multiple contexts from cultured cells to living animals (Mächler et al., 2016; Compan et al., 2015; Plaçais et al., 2017; Delgado et al., 2018; Baeza-Lehnert et al., 2019; Hasel et al., 2017; Rusu et al., 2017).
